fullPassage: The million-dollar question where courage is concerned is whether or not courage can be learned. If fear and courage are to be found at least in part in the hard-wiring of our brains, then it certainly makes sense to assume that there is a genetic component to bravery. If bravery is simply a personality trait, then there isn't much point in trying to learn how to do it better. Fortunately, the research suggests there is hope for people who want to boost their courage quotient. Studies show that people — as many as 82 percent of those studied — overwhelmingly opt to try courage-enhancing strategies to help them face difficult circumstances. Actors who are nervous before opening night spend time on the stage, familiarizing themselves with the auditorium; boxers strut and look angry to overcome the butterflies in their stomachs; people pray or knock on wood or wear favorite pieces of clothing, all because they think this will help to give them a more favorable outcome and allow them to face an uncertain, even risky future.
